title: On the Crisis of Meaning in Classical Christian Education
author: Kyle R. Hughes
summary: Kyle R. Hughes, adapting the introduction to his book Teaching for Truth, Goodness, and Beauty, argues that the classical Christian education movement is growing quickly while still lacking agreement on what "classical" means. Some define it by curriculum (Latin, Great Books, Western civilisation), others by pedagogy, others by its purpose of forming the whole child, and some simply by being the opposite of public schools. He warns that post-Covid growth may include many families who were pushed away from public schools rather than drawn to anything distinctly classical, and that new staff and families who are not enculturated will pull schools toward what is easy, familiar and normal. His proposed remedy is to look to the medieval church, with figures such as Alcuin, Hildegard of Bingen, Dhuoda and Theophilus Presbyter, to recover what truth, goodness and beauty actually mean, since the slogan is now often used loosely. He ends by urging schools not to succumb to compromise but to raise students whose hearts and minds are integrated in one pursuit of God.
points: The movement's rapid growth hides a lack of consensus on whether classical education is defined by curriculum, pedagogy or purpose.
Growth driven by flight from public schools can bring families and staff who are not formed in the philosophy, producing mission drift toward the comfortable.
Hughes treats the slogan "truth, goodness, and beauty" as often hollow: truth reduced to what the Bible says, goodness to therapy language, beauty to opinion.
He proposes recovering medieval Christian teachers as a resource that can give the movement historical depth and theological precision.
The warning is that a classical school that loses what makes it demanding, distinctive and a bit weird trades true education for a comfortable one.
quotes: And yet this period of unmatched growth masks an uncomfortable truth: there is still little consensus on what, exactly, we mean by “classical Christian education.” For some in the movement, the defining quality is curricular, perhaps related to the teaching of Western civilization, Latin, or the Great Books, working towards the goal of students coming to love their cultural inheritance.

Or, if we are being honest, for some, classical Christian education simply means doing the opposite of whatever it is that the public schools are doing—even if the classroom ends up looking like what public schools were doing thirty years ago.
This drift exchanges true education for a comfortable education and threatens the very future of our movement.

The resulting book, Teaching for Truth, Goodness, and Beauty: Medieval Voices for the Future of Classical Christian Education, does not aim at resolving all the differences across various strands of the classical Christian education movement. Instead, I decided to begin from an altogether different starting point: the practices and presuppositions of Christian education in the medieval period.

In working through and applying the thought of each of these medieval figures, I decided to organize my approach around trying to tease out what exactly we mean when we speak of the “transcendentals” of truth, goodness, and beauty.
Goodness, emptied of traditional language of virtue and vice, becomes a cypher for therapeutic language or an idiosyncratic list of personality traits we especially appreciate.

And so, in an increasingly post-Christian landscape, let us raise up a new generation of men and women who, like the medieval writers studied in this book, strive with hearts and minds to taste the truth, goodness, and beauty of King Jesus.
